analysis.one_liner: Imposes FDA regulation, marketing bans, smoke-free rules, and multibillion-dollar fees on tobacco companies to cut youth smoking.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors, the bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in three House committees until the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put tobacco products under Food and Drug Administration control, banned most tobacco advertising including broadcast ads, required smoke-free public buildings, and charged cigarette makers an upfront $10 billion plus 50 cents per unit every year. Most of that money would have funded anti-smoking campaigns, programs to help smokers quit, research, and payments to states, with the rest reducing the federal debt. In exchange, it would have settled a set of class-action "addiction" lawsuits against cigarette makers and created a private arbitration panel to award attorneys' fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, through higher prices, marketing bans, and enforced age limits designed to cut underage smoking; adult smokers who want to quit, through federally funded cessation programs and new Medicaid coverage for quitting; nonsmokers, through smoke-free requirements in public buildings; and state and local governments, which could elect to take settlement-style payments and pass them through to localities. The public would also gain access to the industry's internal documents on health effects, nicotine manipulation, and marketing to kids.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children, smokers trying to quit, nonsmokers

how_it_helps.text: Charges cigarette makers an initial $10 billion (allocated by market share) plus 50 cents per unit manufactured or imported every year, raising prices to discourage child tobacco use, with escalating penalties — carton-only sales and plain black-on-white packaging — for manufacturers that miss mandated youth-use reduction targets.

Gives the FDA authority over tobacco as an addictive drug delivery product, mandates marketing, advertising, and youth-access restrictions modeled on the 1997 settlement framework, bans tobacco advertising on any electronic medium under FCC jurisdiction, and requires stronger warning labels.

Funds a national anti-tobacco public awareness campaign, grants for smoking-cessation programs, research on nicotine addiction, and new Medicaid payments to states for cessation coverage — all paid from the manufacturer fees.
Requires smoke-free environments in public facilities, enforceable by any aggrieved person, state or local agencies, or the EPA, with litigation costs available to prevailing parties.

Creates an independent Tobacco Accountability Board that forces manufacturers to hand over internal documents on health effects, nicotine manipulation, and marketing to children, and makes them public.

Allows states to elect settlement-style payments in lieu of suing manufacturers for tobacco health care costs, requires those payments to be passed through to local governments in proportion to their costs, and ties state grants to adopting a model state tobacco control program with retail licensing and enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, on the hook for an initial $10 billion payment plus 50 cents per unit every year; much of that cost would reach consumers as higher cigarette prices. Retailers face federal and state licensing, inspections, and penalties up to suspension of sales, and broadcasters lose tobacco advertising revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco companies, and smokers via prices

drawbacks.text: The price increases and fees land partly on adult smokers — including low-income smokers, the group least able to absorb regressive price hikes — not just on the companies.

The bill preempts and settles the Castano class-action addiction claims against cigarette makers and hands attorney-fee disputes to a binding, nonappealable arbitration panel whose awards manufacturers must pay and cannot escape in bankruptcy — trading away litigation rights in exchange for the settlement framework.

It repeals the existing federal cigarette labeling laws and bars states from requiring their own warning labels where the Act requires a warning, centralizing all warnings in federal regulation; if federal rules lag, state-level protections would be lost.
The advertising restrictions are expressly barred wherever they would violate the First Amendment, a carve-out that could have blunted the marketing bans in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health stakes were large: tobacco is the leading cause of preventable death, and the bill attacked it with price increases, real FDA authority, marketing bans, funded cessation, smoke-free buildings, and forced disclosure of industry documents. The honest costs are that price increases are regressive for adult smokers who cannot quit, and that the bill bought the framework by settling the Castano addiction litigation and giving plaintiffs' lawyers a guaranteed fee arbitration track — concessions to the industry and the bar built into the design. On balance the trade favored the public, but the litigation settlement and fee arbitration were real prices paid for industry participation.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees on the day it was introduced, then to two subcommittees, and never received a hearing or a vote before the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Martin Meehan introduced the bill on July 31, 1998, near the end of the two-year Congress.
Congress.gov records zero cosponsors, despite the word 'Bipartisan' in the bill's title.
The same day, it was referred to three committees — Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary — splitting jurisdiction and requiring any of them to act before the bill could move.
On August 28, 1998 it was sent to two Commerce subcommittees, Health and Environment and Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 with the bill still in committee, so it died without any vote ever being taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cigarette manufacturers came out ahead: no $10 billion payment, no per-unit fees, no FDA jurisdiction, no marketing bans, and no forced release of internal documents. Tobacco retailers and broadcasters also kept the status quo.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever taken and Congress.gov records zero cosponsors, so the bill's partisan support cannot be measured from the record, despite 'Bipartisan' in its title.

industries.note: On the hook for an initial $10 billion payment, 50 cents per unit annually, FDA control of nicotine, broadcast and marketing bans, and forced public release of internal documents. The one offset: the bill settled the Castano addiction lawsuits and gave manufacturers protection against those specific claims.

Would have faced federal and state retail licensing, compliance inspections, penalties, and authority for the government to suspend or end tobacco sales at violating stores; sales to anyone under 18 would be barred.
Tobacco advertising would be banned outright on any electronic medium under FCC jurisdiction, with broader advertising and promotion restrictions layered on top — lost ad revenue for media outlets.

The bill preempted and settled the Castano addiction claims, ending those lawsuits, but created an arbitration panel guaranteeing a binding route to fee awards paid by manufacturers and protected from bankruptcy discharge.

States could elect settlement-style payments in lieu of suing manufacturers, with mandatory pass-through to local governments; states adopting the model tobacco control program would qualify for annual grants funded by the industry fees.
